title: Bengaluru Firm's Unpaid $672,102 Bill Exposes Payment Risk for Small IT Exporters
excerpt: Ticvic Technologies says an overseas customer tested and accepted its software but has not paid for more than 19 months — a case analysts say shows why small Indian IT exporters must secure payment before delivery.
body:
• A Bengaluru network-software firm, Ticvic Technologies, says it is still owed $672,102 for a completed second-phase project more than 19 months after delivery and customer testing, The Hindu reported.
  • Founder Thiyagu Ganesan says he mortgaged land and pledged gold to keep 47 employees paid; the firm has since shrunk to a few employees.
  • Analysts say a single default can devastate a small exporter, while large firms such as TCS, Infosys and HCLTech have diversified clients and credit-risk systems.
  • Reader utility for small exporters: arrange export-credit cover before delivery, document milestone acceptance in writing, and use the DGFT trade-dispute route and ECGC insurance rather than relying on trust — recovery after delivery is slow and costly.

Deliver the code, then chase the cash. That, in effect, is the trap a Bengaluru technology exporter says it fell into after completing work for an overseas customer that has not paid, according to The Hindu. Ticvic Technologies Pvt Ltd says it is still waiting for $672,102 for a second-phase project completed more than 19 months ago, even though the customer's technical team tested the work and confirmed it was functioning.

The contract shared by Ticvic links payments to milestones and customer acceptance. In an email dated May 29, 2024, a customer representative confirmed the tested function was working, the report said. Ticvic, a network software engineering company with international customers and an overseas project dating back to 2018, says it had been paid for an earlier project and, trusting the relationship, proceeded with the second phase without the expected upfront payment.

The cost fell on the founder personally. Thiyagu Ganesan said he mortgaged land and pledged gold to keep all 47 employees paid, expecting to redeem the assets once the customer settled. Operations have since shrunk significantly, leaving only a few employees, and Ganesan has sought the Karnataka government's intervention. The company says it has also approached China's Ministry of Commerce, the CCPIT Mediation Center and the Indian Embassy in Beijing, without resolving the dispute.

"Winning a $672,000 overseas contract is not a $672,000 export success until you collect the $672,000"

— Phil Fersht, CEO, HFS Research

Why small firms carry the risk

Once software is delivered and accepted, a supplier has surrendered much of its commercial leverage, HFS Research CEO Phil Fersht told The Hindu. Remedies depend largely on the contract — debt recovery, arbitration or litigation, enforcing letters of credit or bank guarantees, or claiming on export-credit insurance arranged beforehand. Cross-border recovery for a claim of $500,000 or $1 million can consume considerable time and money in another country's legal system, he said.

The problem is not described as industry-wide. Gaurav Vasu, founder and CEO of UnearthInsight, said non-payment was not widespread across India's IT services industry, and that large companies have diversified customer bases and sophisticated legal and credit-risk systems. Smaller firms, by contrast, can be devastated by a single default. A chief delivery officer at another technology MSME told the paper firms typically rely on legal counsel, collection agencies and negotiation rather than government intervention, and that his company is trying to recover about $1 million, with talks under way to accept equity in the customer's business instead of litigating.

The protection that has to be bought before delivery

India does have mechanisms, but they work best when set up at the start. The Directorate General of Foreign Trade's trade-dispute mechanism covers non-payment involving goods, services and technology, and the Export Credit Guarantee Corporation (ECGC) offers insurance for software and technology exports, The Hindu noted. Fersht's point was preventive: buyer due diligence, documented acceptance criteria, proper records and a correctly structured transaction matter more than any remedy after the fact.

ECGC cover itself has been expanding in other export sectors. At a session on October 12, ECGC outlined that, effective July 1, 2026, it raised the ceiling under its Whole Turnover Export Credit Insurance for Banks cover from Rs 100 crore to Rs 300 crore per exporter or group, and lifted normal bank cover from 50% to 75%, according to GJEPC's Solitaire magazine. That session covered gems and jewellery, not software, but it shows policy moving toward more insured headroom against overseas-buyer non-payment, if cover is arranged in advance.

What this means for diaspora-linked firms

Many small Indian IT exporters sell through diaspora networks abroad, where trust can wrongly substitute for payment security. The lesson from Ticvic's case is narrow and practical: a tested, accepted delivery is not revenue. Milestone payments, acceptance records, a letter of credit or guarantee, and export-credit cover arranged before work begins are the difference between a bad debt and a business-ending one. Whether the Karnataka government, Indian Embassy channels or mediation produce Ticvic's $672,102 is now the test case other small exporters will watch.
